title: The 2026 Iran War — A Global Cascade

scenes.narration: January 2026. Backchannel negotiations between Washington and Tehran are collapsing. The Geneva talks — the last diplomatic thread — snap over uranium enrichment limits. The window for a deal closes.
February 28, 2026. Operation Epic Fury. U.S. and Israeli forces launch simultaneous strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, missile sites, and command infrastructure. The war begins before dawn.

Within hours of the first strikes, Iran closes the Strait of Hormuz. 20% of the world's oil — 20 million barrels per day — stops moving. One-third of global fertilizer shipments are trapped. The IEA calls it the largest supply disruption in oil market history.

The Strait of Hormuz. Just 21 nautical miles wide at its narrowest point. To the north: Iran's mountainous coast and missile batteries. To the south: Oman and the UAE. This single passage carries 21 million barrels of oil daily — one-fifth of global consumption. Tankers squeeze through shipping lanes just two miles wide, bordered by Iranian waters on one side and Omani waters on the other. A single missile, a single mine, a single sunken hull could close it for weeks.

The Gulf producers go dark. Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Iraq, and Qatar lose their primary export route. Storage fills. Tankers wait at anchor. Gulf production collapses by 10 million barrels per day within two weeks.
Brent crude surges from $64 to $119.50 a barrel in days — the sharpest spike since 1973. QatarEnergy declares force majeure on all LNG exports. Natural gas prices in Europe rise 75% in a single week.

Asia absorbs the deepest shock. China, India, Japan, and South Korea together receive 75% of Gulf oil and 59% of Gulf LNG. With supply severed, parts of Asia impose four-day work weeks and ban air conditioning use.

Iran makes a calculated asymmetric move: it selectively allows Chinese tankers to transit the Strait — for a price. Yuan-settled payments become the access condition. China secures energy; U.S. allies are locked out. A new fracture in the global energy order is written in a single decree.

February 28, opening hours of the war. A U.S. strike hits the Shajareh Tayyiba elementary school in Minab, southern Iran. At least 168 children are killed — most of them girls aged 7 to 12. Hours later, a sports hall in Lamerd is struck, killing teenage girls at training.

By Week 2, Israel launches an assassination campaign. Ali Larijani — head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council — is killed. On the same day, Basij commander Gholamreza Soleimani is assassinated. Israel says the strikes are designed to provoke an uprising. Iran's government vows to fight to the end.

Supreme Leader Khamenei is killed in a strike on Tehran. His son Mojtaba is rapidly named successor. In his first public statement as Supreme Leader, Mojtaba declares the Hormuz closure must continue as 'a tool to pressure the enemy.' The strait closure is now official state policy — not a battlefield side effect.

Iran retaliates across nine countries simultaneously. Drone and missile strikes hit Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Israel. Oman's Salalah port fuel tanks are struck. 18 are killed, including 3 U.S. servicemen. Bahrain's government deploys foreign riot police to suppress domestic unrest.

Lebanon re-enters the war. Hezbollah launches a major rocket barrage into northern Israel. Israel issues sweeping displacement orders south of the Zahrani River and kills dozens in Lebanese strikes. Spain permanently withdraws its ambassador to Israel. The conflict spreads its third front.

The fertilizer shock arrives just as Northern Hemisphere spring planting begins. One-third of the world's fertilizer transited Hormuz. U.S. ammonia prices are up 41%, urea up 21%. Illinois farmers cannot get nitrogen suppliers to commit to a price. The fertilizer price index surges 31% in 28 days.

Brazil sits at the end of the supply chain but absorbs the full force. It produces 60% of global soybean exports and depends on Hormuz for nearly half its fertilizer. If nitrogen collapses, Brazilian yields fall. Global food prices face a second shock wave in Q3 2026 — months after the energy spike.

Sudan and Somalia face immediate food emergencies. Sudan imports 80%+ of its wheat through routes now disrupted. Somalia has already seen food prices rise 20%. The WFP warns 45 million more people could be forced into acute food insecurity if the war continues. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia are the most exposed.

Australia faces the most structurally exposed position of any Western nation. It holds only 50–60 days of liquid fuel reserves — well below the IEA's 90-day requirement. It imports 90% of its refined petroleum. Its two operating refineries, Ampol Brisbane and Viva Geelong, are the only domestic buffer.

Australia's AUKUS alliance is an active liability. Its naval assets are committed to U.S. operations in the Indo-Pacific and Persian Gulf — the very theatre that has cut off Australia's fuel supply. Australia is paying the cost of the war it cannot afford to oppose and cannot afford to support.

Qantas raises international fares as jet fuel surges 150% in two weeks — from $85 to $150–200/barrel. Virgin Australia cancels 22 Qatar Airways codeshare flights to Doha. Australia's only Middle East air corridor is severed. International arrivals had already fallen 8.2% in February.

Russia watches from the sidelines. Isolated by Ukraine sanctions, it sees oil prices spike — but its own customer base is scrambling for non-Gulf alternatives that bypass Moscow too. Russia's oil export revenues fall despite the price spike. Moscow weighs 10% budget cuts.

The clear winners: non-Gulf oil producers. The U.S. (ExxonMobil, Chevron), Canada, Norway, and Australia's Santos and Woodside are generating windfall revenues. American refiners — Valero, Marathon, Phillips 66 — are capturing record crack spreads. The energy sector's gain is everyone else's cost.

In Washington, the War Powers Resolution fails 212 to 219 in the House on March 5. A new WPR vote is expected this week. Democrats are split: some want the war ended; others quietly see electoral advantage in letting Trump own a failing conflict into the 2026 midterms.

Trump claims Iran is calling to negotiate. Iran calls it 'a huge lie.' Senior Iranian officials say no talks are possible until a new Supreme Leader formally consolidates power. Mojtaba has already spoken: the Strait stays closed. Diplomacy is frozen.

Week 4. Day 25. The IEA has released a record 400 million barrels from strategic reserves — and calls it 'not the solution.' 3.2 million Iranians are displaced. Chicago gas averages $4.46/gallon. Australian fuel supplies are secure only through late April. The world is burning through its buffers.
